## Before starting

**Ungraded practice; no submission.** In this lab, we'll estimate support for the 2010 Irish budget with Wordscores and Wordfish. We'll compare their rankings, read a speech on which they disagree, and check what changes when we choose another reference text. Allow **60–75 minutes**, including time to read the speeches and discuss the outputs.

We download and extract the [**Lab ZIP**](https://github.com/davidycliao/NTLDEV-7191-1151/raw/refs/heads/main/W7/downloads/week7-lab.zip), open **`Lab_Session_W7.R`** in RStudio, and read this handout alongside it. We keep `Data/` beside the R script and run **S01–S08b, including all lettered substeps, in one R session**. We can read this HTML offline; Quarto is needed only if we choose to edit and render the source QMD.

[R script](Lab_Session_W7.R) · [Instructions](README.md) · [W7 student slides](https://raw.githack.com/davidycliao/NTLDEV-7191-1151/main/W7/slide/week7.html)

After each code block, we'll read the actual output and discuss what it lets us conclude. The outputs below were generated by executing all seventeen checkpoints in order with **quanteda 4.3.1**, **quanteda.textmodels 0.9.10**, one processing thread, and seed **7197** before Wordfish. With other versions, we may see small numerical differences. We can bring questions to [instructor](https://calendly.com/ycliao/text-as-data-instructor) or [TA](https://calendly.com/ycliao/text-as-data-ta) office hours.

### From W6 classification to W7 measurement

In W6, we compared predicted categories with reference labels. Here we ask whether a continuous position captures support for a particular budget. We'll use agreement between models, close reading, and reference sensitivity to examine that interpretation. We would need independent judgments to assess how well the positions measure budget support.

## Reading the R code

We'll work from top to bottom in the same R session. In RStudio, we select a line or block and use **Ctrl+Enter** on Windows or **Cmd+Enter** on Mac. The checkpoint names match the W7 slides and `W7_scaling.R`, so we can move between the handout and the classroom demonstration.

| Syntax | What we do with it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `<-` | Save a result under a name | `counts <- dfm(toks_irish)` |
| `$` | Read a data-frame column or model component | `results$ws_raw`, `wf$theta` |
| `[rows, columns]` | Select observations or variables | `results[is.na(results$reference), ]` |
| `NA` | Leave a reference position unknown | `rep(NA_real_, ndoc(counts))` |
| `match()` | Find row or column positions by ID or name | `match(ref_ids, meta$doc_id)` |
| `&` | Keep rows satisfying both conditions | `is.na(ref_scores) & is.na(ref_alt)` |
| `rank()` | Order scores within the selected texts | `rank(comparison$ws_raw)` |
| `#` | Write a comment that R does not execute | `# S03: Define the Wordscores references` |

### Functions used in the lab

| Task | Functions or components | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Read corpus metadata and text | `docvars()`, `docnames()`, `corpus_reshape()` | quanteda |
| Count words | `tokens()`, `tokens_tolower()`, `dfm()` | quanteda |
| Match a scoring vocabulary | `dfm_match()`, `ntoken()` | quanteda |
| Fit and predict Wordscores | `textmodel_wordscores()`, `coef()`, `predict()` | quanteda.textmodels / R generics |
| Fit and inspect Wordfish | `textmodel_wordfish()`, `$theta`, `$se.theta`, `$beta`, `$psi` | quanteda.textmodels |
| Compare and plot estimates | `rank()`, `cor()`, `plot()`, `text()` | base R |

## Data and the measurement question

We use the fourteen speeches in `quanteda.textmodels::data_corpus_irishbudget2010`. They concern the **2010 budget**, debated in **December 2009**. We load this corpus directly from the package. `Data/irish_budget2010.csv` contains a copy of the original texts and metadata for reading or reuse; we do not need to import it to run the script.

Our unit is a **speech**, and our intended dimension is **support for this budget**. We retain party labels to help interpret the results. We supply neither party labels nor independent human position scores to the model-fitting functions.

| Method | What we supply | What we need to examine |
|---|---|---|
| Wordscores | Word counts and two reference speeches assigned −1 and +1 | Whether the references identify budget support and provide relevant language for the other speeches |
| Wordfish | Word counts; an ordering to fix the direction | Whether one dimension of word-use variation corresponds to budget support |

For Wordscores, we'll assign **Lenihan +1** and **Bruton −1**. These are our reference inputs for this debate. For Wordfish, we'll request **Bruton below Lenihan** to fix the sign. That ordering does not give Wordfish a set of reference position scores.

We remove punctuation, symbols and numbers, and lowercase a working copy. We retain stopwords and use **counts without stemming, trimming or TF-IDF weighting**. We keep the original corpus for reading quotations and surrounding arguments. Both methods begin with the same count matrix; Wordscores prediction later uses the vocabulary scored by its references.

## 1. Set up R and inspect the corpus

If the two packages are not installed yet, we run this command once before S01. Installation messages depend on our system.

```r
install.packages(c("quanteda", "quanteda.textmodels"),
  repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
```

### S01. Packages and the Irish corpus

We load the packages, suppress their startup messages, use one processing thread, and keep the built-in corpus as `corp_irish`. We print the package versions before counting documents.

```{r}
#| label: s01
# S01: Packages and the built-in corpus
# install.packages(c("quanteda", "quanteda.textmodels"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(quanteda)
  library(quanteda.textmodels)
})
quanteda_options(threads = 1)
options(width = 72, digits = 4)
corp_irish <- data_corpus_irishbudget2010
c(quanteda = as.character(packageVersion("quanteda")),
  textmodels = as.character(packageVersion("quanteda.textmodels")))
ndoc(corp_irish)
```

**Read the output.** We see the two package versions and fourteen documents. We keep this session open because the later steps reuse the objects created here.

**Discuss.** What does one document represent in this analysis, and why do we record the package versions?

### S02a. Speakers and document IDs

We copy the speaker and party metadata into `meta` and give each document a short ID derived from its original speech number. We use these IDs when we select references and join model results.

```{r}
#| label: s02a
# S02a: Speakers and stable document IDs
meta <- data.frame(
  doc_id = paste0("ie_", docvars(corp_irish, "number")),
  speaker = docvars(corp_irish, "name"),
  party = docvars(corp_irish, "party"))
docnames(corp_irish) <- meta$doc_id
print(meta, row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** We have fourteen speaker rows, with IDs `ie_01`–`ie_14`. Lenihan and Bruton are the first two speeches. We retain party as metadata; the fitting functions receive word counts rather than this party column.

**Discuss.** Which fields do we use to keep texts and scores aligned, and which fields could help us interpret a position?

### S02b. Tokenize a working copy

We remove punctuation, symbols and numbers, then lowercase the tokens. We inspect the first twelve tokens from the first speech. We leave `corp_irish` unchanged for close reading later.

```{r}
#| label: s02b
# S02b: Tokenize a working copy
toks_irish <- tokens(corp_irish, remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE)
toks_irish <- tokens_tolower(toks_irish)
head(as.list(toks_irish)[[1]], 12)
```

**Read the output.** The output begins with Lenihan's words, now in lowercase and separated into tokens. Our later count matrix will not retain their sequence or the punctuation marking a quotation.

**Discuss.** What information about a speaker's use of quoted language do we lose when we count these tokens?

### S02c. Build the count matrix

We count the tokens, inspect the matrix dimensions, check for empty documents, and read the six most frequent features.

```{r}
#| label: s02c
# S02c: Build the common count matrix
counts <- dfm(toks_irish)
dim(counts)
any(ntoken(counts) == 0)
topfeatures(counts, 6)
```

**Read the output.** We have **14 rows and 4,885 columns**. The empty-document check is `FALSE`. Common words such as `the` remain in the matrix; frequency alone does not tell us whether a word distinguishes positions.

**Discuss.** What does one cell count, and how do we distinguish a frequent word from a word associated with a position?

## 2. Estimate positions with Wordscores

We first use two reference speeches to score words, check the vocabulary available for prediction, and read the resulting raw document scores.

### S03. Define the Wordscores references

We create a named vector of unknown scores, then assign Lenihan +1 and Bruton −1 by document ID. We print the two assignments to check the design before fitting.

```{r}
#| label: s03
# S03: Define the Wordscores references
ref_scores <- rep(NA_real_, ndoc(counts))
names(ref_scores) <- docnames(counts)
ref_ids <- c("ie_01", "ie_02")
ref_scores[ref_ids] <- c(1, -1)
print(data.frame(speaker = meta$speaker[match(ref_ids, meta$doc_id)],
  reference = ref_scores[ref_ids]), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** We see the two assigned endpoints. The other twelve entries remain `NA`, meaning that we have not supplied their positions as Wordscores references. These assignments establish our intended budget-support direction.

**Discuss.** What evidence from the speeches would we use to defend these two reference choices, and what does `NA` mean in this vector?

### S04a. Fit Wordscores and inspect word scores

We fit Wordscores with `smooth = 0` and inspect six words. The model learns their scores from relative word use in the selected reference speeches.

```{r}
#| label: s04a
# S04a: Fit Wordscores and inspect word scores
ws <- textmodel_wordscores(counts, y = ref_scores, smooth = 0)
probe_words <- c("budget", "government", "tax",
                 "jobs", "fair", "recovery")
print(data.frame(word = probe_words,
  score = round(coef(ws)[probe_words], 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** We see `fair` at −0.229 and `tax` at +0.665. These values describe associations with our two references. We have not supplied a general sentiment dictionary, so an ordinarily positive word can point toward the negative reference.

**Discuss.** How would we explain the negative score for `fair` without treating it as a negative sentiment word?

### S04b. Check the scoring vocabulary

We match the count matrix to words that received a Wordscores coefficient. For each speech, we divide its retained token count by its original processed token count.

```{r}
#| label: s04b
# S04b: Align the scoring vocabulary and inspect coverage
ws_counts <- dfm_match(counts, features = names(coef(ws)))
ws_coverage <- ntoken(ws_counts) / ntoken(counts)
dim(ws_counts)
summary(ws_coverage)
```

**Read the output.** The scoring matrix has **2,131 features**, compared with 4,885 in the full DFM. Coverage ranges from **0.836 to 1.000**. With `smooth = 0`, words absent from the reference vocabulary do not receive scores. Coverage counts token occurrences, rather than unique word types.

**Discuss.** If we retain about 84% of a speech's processed tokens, what have we learned about coverage, and what would we still need to know about validity?

### S04c. Predict raw Wordscores

We predict every speech using the matched vocabulary and `rescaling = "none"`. We keep the assigned inputs in `reference` and the predictions in `ws_raw` so we can compare their roles.

```{r}
#| label: s04c
# S04c: Predict raw Wordscores for every speech
ws_pred <- predict(ws, newdata = ws_counts, rescaling = "none")
results <- meta
results$reference <- ref_scores
results$ws_raw <- as.numeric(ws_pred)
results$coverage <- ws_coverage
print(data.frame(speaker = results$speaker, party = results$party,
  reference = results$reference,
  ws_raw = round(results$ws_raw, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** Lenihan and Bruton are rescored at approximately **+0.339 and −0.339**, even though we assigned +1 and −1. Averaging learned word scores over shared language pulls raw scores toward the centre. The twelve `NA`-reference speeches are new texts for Wordscores; rescoring the two references does not provide an independent benchmark.

**Discuss.** Why do we get predicted reference scores inside the assigned endpoints, and what would be misleading about calling their agreement validation?

## 3. Estimate positions with Wordfish

We now fit a single dimension from all fourteen speeches without a reference-score vector. Under the Poisson specification, expected word counts depend on document effects, word baselines and a word-loading-by-position term. We need to examine whether that dimension captures our substantive question.

### S05a. Fit Wordfish and set its direction

We use the full count matrix and find the Bruton–Lenihan row indices from their IDs. We set seed 7197 and fit the Poisson Wordfish model with that ordering in `dir`.

```{r}
#| label: s05a
# S05a: Fit Wordfish and fix its orientation
wf_dir <- match(c("ie_02", "ie_01"), docnames(counts))
set.seed(7197)
wf <- textmodel_wordfish(counts, dir = wf_dir,
  dispersion = "poisson")
data.frame(speaker = meta$speaker[wf_dir],
  theta = round(wf$theta[wf_dir], 3))
```

**Read the output.** We see Bruton below Lenihan, at approximately **−0.585 and +1.775**. Wordfish estimates all positions jointly. We have fixed its direction; we have not supplied the Wordscores reference vector or established the meaning of the fitted dimension.

**Discuss.** What does our `dir` choice identify numerically, and what evidence would we need before calling the resulting dimension budget support?

### S05b. Read positions and model standard errors

We add the estimated positions and their standard errors to `results`, keeping the original speaker order. These standard errors describe uncertainty under the fitted model and its assumptions.

```{r}
#| label: s05b
# S05b: Inspect Wordfish positions and model standard errors
results$wf_theta <- wf$theta
results$wf_se <- wf$se.theta
print(data.frame(speaker = results$speaker, party = results$party,
  theta = round(results$wf_theta, 3),
  se = round(results$wf_se, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** Burton has the lowest estimated position, at about **−1.150**, with a model standard error of about **0.016**. We can estimate a position precisely under the model while still needing evidence about what that position means.

**Discuss.** If we see small standard errors, which uncertainty have we summarized, and which questions about the budget-support interpretation remain?

### S05c. Read word discrimination and baseline frequency

We inspect `beta` and `psi` for the same six words used in S04a. `beta` links word use to position; `psi` is the word baseline in the log expected-count model, alongside the document effect.

```{r}
#| label: s05c
# S05c: Inspect word discrimination and baseline frequency
word_id <- match(probe_words, wf$features)
print(data.frame(word = probe_words,
  beta = round(wf$beta[word_id], 3),
  psi = round(wf$psi[word_id], 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** We see separate estimates for discrimination and baseline frequency. For example, `budget` has a relatively large baseline and a small loading. The positive loading for `fair` also differs from its negative Wordscores value, because the two models learn their parameters in different ways.

**Discuss.** How do we distinguish a word's baseline frequency, its association with the Wordfish position, and its everyday evaluative meaning?

## 4. Compare the models and return to the speeches

We use agreement to describe the rankings and disagreement to guide our reading. We would need evidence beyond agreement between these two models to validate budget support.

### S06a. Compare the twelve new texts

We exclude the two Wordscores references, rank the remaining twelve speeches within each model, and sort by the absolute rank gap. We use document ID to break ties in the display order.

```{r}
#| label: s06a
# S06a: Compare rankings among the twelve new texts
comparison <- results[is.na(results$reference), ]
comparison$ws_rank <- rank(comparison$ws_raw)
comparison$wf_rank <- rank(comparison$wf_theta)
comparison$gap <- abs(comparison$ws_rank - comparison$wf_rank)
comparison <- comparison[order(-comparison$gap, comparison$doc_id), ]
round(cor(comparison$ws_raw, comparison$wf_theta,
  method = "spearman"), 3)
print(head(comparison[c("speaker", "ws_rank", "wf_rank", "gap")], 6),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** Spearman rank correlation is **0.734**. Burton has the largest rank gap: **Wordscores rank 7, Wordfish rank 1**, a gap of 6. Rank 1 is the lower end of each oriented scale. We are comparing model rankings on the same corpus; these twelve speeches were still included in the Wordfish fit.

**Discuss.** How can we see substantial overall rank agreement and still find a large disagreement about one speech? Why would we avoid calling 0.734 an accuracy score?

### S06b. Plot the two scales

We plot each of the twelve new texts using its raw Wordscores value and Wordfish position. We label the three speeches selected by the rank-gap diagnostic in S06a.

```{r}
#| label: s06b
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-dpi: 150
#| fig-alt: "Twelve speeches on raw Wordscores and Wordfish axes; Burton, ODonnell and Ryan are labelled."
#| fig-cap: "The twelve new texts for Wordscores, labelled by the three largest rank gaps. Wordfish was fitted to all fourteen speeches."
# S06b: Plot the new texts on both scales
plot(comparison$ws_raw, comparison$wf_theta,
  pch = 19, col = "#0271bb", xlim = c(-0.08, 0.24),
  xlab = "Wordscores (raw)", ylab = "Wordfish (theta)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey80", lty = 3)
text(comparison$ws_raw[1:3], comparison$wf_theta[1:3],
  labels = comparison$speaker[1:3], pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
```

**Read the output.** We see Burton, O'Donnell and Ryan labelled. The horizontal and vertical axes have different units, and their zero lines do not define a validated neutral position. The plot helps us choose cases to read rather than settle which model is correct.

**Discuss.** Which relationship can we compare in this plot, and why would we avoid reading a one-unit distance on one axis in the units of the other?

### S07a. Read the largest ranking disagreement

We select the largest rank gap using `comparison`, then return to the original corpus. We split that speech into sentences and read its opening in the original wording.

```{r}
#| label: s07a
# S07a: Identify and read the largest ranking disagreement
read_id <- comparison$doc_id[1]
print(comparison[1, c("doc_id", "speaker", "ws_rank", "wf_rank")],
  row.names = FALSE)
read_sentences <- as.character(corpus_reshape(
  corp_irish[read_id], to = "sentences"))
cat(strwrap(read_sentences[1], width = 66), sep = "\n")
```

**Read the output.** Our diagnostic selects **Joan Burton (`ie_03`)**. The opening reports a Goldman Sachs note about consensus. We need to distinguish the source of that claim from Burton's own stance and read how she develops the argument.

**Discuss.** Whose claim about consensus are we reading, and how might Burton use it in an argument about the budget?

### S07b. Read the surrounding argument

We read sentences 5–7 of the same speech. With the current data and settings, these passages follow Burton's opening. If our fit selects another speech, we first check which surrounding passages we should read.

```{r}
#| label: s07b
# S07b: Read more of the same speech
# In this corpus, the selected speech is Burton's. Read sentences 5-7.
cat(strwrap(paste(read_sentences[5:7], collapse = " "),
  width = 66), sep = "\n")
# We can print the full speech in the console:
# cat(as.character(corp_irish[read_id]))
```

**Read the output.** Burton describes a missed opportunity for shared burdens and criticizes the budget. This context gives us reason to question whether a middle score represents moderate support. It does not by itself show which words caused the disagreement between the two models.

**Discuss.** How does this passage affect our interpretation of Burton's position, and what else would we read before judging either model?

## 5. Check sensitivity to a reference choice

We change one reference while keeping the remaining analysis choices fixed. We then compare the same set of new speeches under both designs.

### S08a. Change the positive reference

We replace Lenihan with Cowen at +1 and retain Bruton at −1. We use the same preprocessing, `smooth = 0`, vocabulary-matching rule and raw prediction setting.

```{r}
#| label: s08a
# S08a: Replace the positive reference and refit Wordscores
ref_alt <- ref_scores
ref_alt[c("ie_01", "ie_05")] <- c(NA, 1)
ws_alt <- textmodel_wordscores(counts, y = ref_alt, smooth = 0)
ws_alt_counts <- dfm_match(counts, features = names(coef(ws_alt)))
ws_alt_pred <- predict(ws_alt, newdata = ws_alt_counts,
  rescaling = "none")
print(data.frame(speaker = meta$speaker[!is.na(ref_alt)],
  reference = ref_alt[!is.na(ref_alt)]), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** The printed reference design now contains **Bruton −1 and Cowen +1**. Even with unchanged numerical endpoints, we have changed the positive reference's lexical evidence. The refit can therefore change both word scores and vocabulary coverage.

**Discuss.** Which part of our measurement design changes when we replace a reference speech but keep its assigned endpoint at +1?

### S08b. Compare the same eleven new texts

We retain only speeches with unknown reference scores in both designs. We exclude Lenihan, Bruton and Cowen, then recompute both rankings within the same eleven texts. We calculate `change` as the new rank minus the earlier rank.

```{r}
#| label: s08b
# S08b: Compare ranks within the same eleven new texts
common_new <- is.na(ref_scores) & is.na(ref_alt)
sensitivity <- meta[common_new, c("doc_id", "speaker")]
sensitivity$before <- rank(ws_pred[common_new])
sensitivity$after <- rank(ws_alt_pred[common_new])
sensitivity$change <- sensitivity$after - sensitivity$before
print(sensitivity[c("speaker", "before", "after", "change")],
  row.names = FALSE)
```

**Read the output.** Ryan moves from rank **6 to 9** and O'Caolain from **10 to 7**, the largest changes in this comparison. A positive change means movement toward the higher end of the ranking. These ranks use eleven common texts, rather than the twelve-text comparison in S06. We hold membership fixed so that reference sensitivity is not confused with a change in the comparison set.

**Discuss.** Which conclusions would we retain after this check, and how would we describe the rankings that depend on our reference choice?

## 6. Report what we can conclude

We write a short account of the analysis, using the output and the original speeches together:

1. **Define the target and unit.** What do we intend to measure, and what does one document represent?
2. **Describe our design.** Which preprocessing, references and orientation did we use? Which estimates are raw Wordscores and which are Wordfish positions?
3. **Report agreement and disagreement.** How do we describe the 0.734 rank correlation alongside Burton's rank gap and the passages we read?
4. **Report sensitivity.** Which rankings changed after we replaced Lenihan with Cowen, and which eleven speeches did we compare?
5. **Specify independent evidence.** How would we collect human judgments of budget support without giving readers our model scores? What would we ask them to compare, and which additional speeches would we read?

We have diagnosed model disagreement and reference sensitivity. To validate the interpretation of the scale, we would compare the estimates with independent evidence about budget support. We also distinguish the Wordfish model standard errors from uncertainty about whether the dimension measures our intended concept.

## Data notes

We can inspect the full original speeches in `Data/irish_budget2010.csv`. The file contains `doc_id`, `speaker`, `party`, `budget_year`, `source_document` and `text`. We retain the corpus wording and punctuation. We assign the −1/+1 reference inputs in the R script; the CSV does not provide independently validated position scores. The [data README](Data/README.md) records the source and fields.

We use the installed package corpus for fitting, one processing thread, and seed 7197 immediately before Wordfish. We compare the models on the supplied corpus. Our preprocessing and fitted results are classroom estimates, so we distinguish them from estimates reported in the original articles.

## Reading connections

- **Wordscores:** [Laver, Benoit and Garry (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055403000698). We connect the reference design to word scores and raw document scoring in S03–S04c.
- **Wordfish:** [Slapin and Proksch (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2008.00338.x). We distinguish identification, word loadings and model precision from the interpretation of positions in S05a–S05c.
- **Human validation:** [Lowe and Benoit (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt002), “Validating Estimates of Latent Traits from Textual Data Using Human Judgment as a Benchmark.” We use the Irish budget case to motivate close reading and independent evidence in S06–S08.
- **Lecture concepts:** [Benoit, TCD text-scaling lecture (2018)](https://kenbenoit.net/assets/courses/tcd2018qta/QTA_TCD_Day5.pdf). We can review pp. 9–20 for Wordscores, pp. 37–41 for Wordfish, and pp. 59–66 for validity, uncertainty and text scope. The lecture's Gormley example and our Burton diagnostic concern different passages.
